analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare to automatically cover new FDA "breakthrough" medical devices for four years.
analysis.headline: Despite 33 bipartisan cosponsors, the bill never received a hearing or a vote and died in a House subcommittee when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require Medicare to pay for any medical device that goes through the FDA's expedited "breakthrough" review, treating it as medically necessary for four years without the usual Medicare evidence review. Medicare would have to assign the device a billing code within three months of FDA approval and pay extra hospital charges for it, even for devices with no existing Medicare payment category. In practice, it front-loads payment to device makers before anyone establishes that the devices work or are worth their price.
analysis.who_benefits: Medical device manufacturers gain the most: guaranteed billing codes within three months of FDA clearance, four years of Medicare payment deemed "reasonable and necessary," extra inpatient and outpatient hospital payments based on list or invoice prices, and coverage even for devices with no existing Medicare benefit category. Medicare patients with life-threatening or disabling conditions would also gain faster access to new devices, before the slower coverage process would normally allow it.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Device makers, and Medicare patients seeking faster access

how_it_helps.text: Device makers would get a unique Medicare billing code within three months of FDA approval or clearance, ending the long wait that can follow FDA clearance under normal Medicare rules.

During a four-year transitional period, each breakthrough device would be deemed "reasonable and necessary" by law, so Medicare would have to cover it without making its own judgment about whether it works.

The bill would also deem devices eligible for extra hospital payments — add-on payments under the inpatient system and pass-through payments under the outpatient system — with the payment amount based on the most recent cost data, which can include the manufacturer's list and invoice prices.

Devices with no existing Medicare benefit category at all would be covered and paid during the transitional period, with the Secretary reporting to Congress afterward rather than proving value up front.

For patients, the practical upside is earlier access: someone with a life-threatening or irreversibly debilitating condition could get a newly cleared device through Medicare roughly as soon as the FDA signs off, rather than after a separate Medicare coverage review.

analysis.who_pays: The Medicare program — meaning taxpayers and beneficiaries through premiums and cost-sharing — would bear the cost of paying for four years of device use before any Medicare review of clinical effectiveness, including devices cleared through the lighter 510(k) process that does not require proof of clinical benefit. Patients who receive a device that later proves ineffective would bear that risk directly. The bill contains no financing offset.
analysis.who_pays_short: Medicare, taxpayers, and beneficiaries through premiums

drawbacks.text: The bill would force Medicare to treat breakthrough devices as "reasonable and necessary" for four years even when they were cleared through the FDA's 510(k) pathway, which does not require clinical-trial evidence of patient benefit — so the program would pay, and beneficiaries would share costs, before anyone knows whether the device works.

If the Secretary does not act within two years of a device's approval, coverage after the transitional period automatically extends to every FDA-approved indication, shifting the burden onto Medicare to restrict coverage rather than onto manufacturers to prove value.

Devices with no existing Medicare benefit category would be covered and paid during the transitional period based only on reports to Congress afterward, and the bill sets no budget offset for the added spending — costs would land on the Medicare trust funds and on beneficiaries' premiums.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real benefit: faster access to genuinely new technology for Medicare patients with serious illnesses, where today's coverage process can add a year or more after FDA clearance. But the bill buys that access by waiving Medicare's evidence review entirely for four years, paying at list or invoice prices, and defaulting to broad coverage afterward unless the agency affirmatively narrows it. That design would shift the risk of paying for unproven devices onto taxpayers and beneficiaries, which is why the Medicare agency pulled back from a similar administrative rule. A better version would condition automatic coverage on real-world evidence collection with teeth — this bill collects data but pays regardless of what it shows.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in June 2021, sent to two House committees and a health subcommittee, and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Representative Suzan DelBene introduced the bill on June 22, 2021, with a bipartisan group of original cosponsors including Republicans Jackie Walorski, Gus Bilirakis, and Fred Upton.
The same day, it was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee, and both referrals were passed down to the Health Subcommittee.

The bill gathered 33 cosponsors — 18 Democrats and 15 Republicans — but the action record shows nothing after the subcommittee referral: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor action through the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023.

Its key provision — automatic Medicare payment for FDA breakthrough devices — closely tracked an administrative rule the Medicare agency itself had moved away from, and no version of the idea advanced in the 117th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo at Medicare came out ahead: CMS keeps the authority to weigh clinical evidence and cost before paying for a new device. Device makers and hospitals lost a guaranteed four-year payment channel, while some patients with serious conditions lost a possible route to earlier access.

sides.party_line_note: Support was genuinely bipartisan — 18 of the 33 cosponsors were Democrats and 15 were Republicans, and the bill died without any recorded opposition vote because no vote ever happened.

industries.note: The bill guarantees device makers a Medicare billing code within three months and four years of payment at prices based on their own list and invoice prices, without Medicare first finding the device effective. Their gain comes directly out of the Medicare program's budget — and patients' premiums — before anyone proves the device is worth it.

Hospitals would be deemed eligible for extra add-on payments under the inpatient system and pass-through payments under the outpatient system whenever they furnish a breakthrough device, with the rules applied retroactively to discharges from late 2019 and 2020. Because hospitals are paid for delivering devices patients want, their interest in this bill runs alongside patients' access interest.

The program would lose the ability to ask whether a new device works before paying for it for four years, and beneficiaries' premiums and cost-sharing would rise with the added spending. Patients would gain faster access, but they would also share the cost of devices that may never be shown to help.
